blocks.title: What the interviewer is really testing
blocks.text: Not whether you can print `010203`. That is trivial single-threaded. The test is: **can you impose a deterministic global order on non-deterministic threads without busy-waiting, deadlock, or lost wakeups?** Your choice of primitive, your invariant, and how you shut the extra threads down is the entire interview. The output string is just the oracle.
The problem

You get `n >= 1`. Three threads share one instance. Thread A repeatedly calls `zero(printNumber)`, thread B calls `even(printNumber)`, thread C calls `odd(printNumber)`. You must coordinate them so the visible output is exactly `0 1 0 2 0 3 ... 0 n` — that is `2*n` prints total, always starting with `0` and strictly alternating zero and counting number. Threads start in arbitrary order and the scheduler can preempt anywhere. `printNumber` itself is not thread-safe for ordering; you supply the ordering.

items: `ZeroEvenOdd(int n)` — stores the bound. `n` is the last number to print, not a count of zeros. For `n=1` output is `01`.
`void zero(printNumber)` — called in a loop `n` times by its thread. Must print `0` exactly `n` times, once before each `i`.
`void even(printNumber)` — called in a loop by its thread. Must print `2,4,6,... <= n` in order, one at a time, each preceded by a `0`.
`void odd(printNumber)` — called in a loop by its thread. Must print `1,3,5,... <= n` in order, one at a time, each preceded by a `0`.

Constraint that matters: only one thread may be *logically runnable* at a time. Zero runs, then exactly one of odd/even runs, then zero again. Two number threads must never both proceed on the same slot.

blocks.text: Clarify before you code

Strong candidates spend three minutes pinning the contract because every ambiguity becomes a race or a hang later. Do not assume LeetCode's harness. In a real codebase `n` can be zero, threads can be interrupted, and `printNumber` can throw. Lock those answers in, then the state machine is forced.

items.title: Who loops, and how many times?
items.text: Confirm each method contains its own loop: `zero` loops `n` times, `odd` loops over odd `i <= n`, `even` loops over even `i <= n`. You do not get one call per print from outside. This decides where termination logic lives.

items.title: What primitives am I allowed?
items.text: Ask: `Semaphore`, `ReentrantLock + Condition`, `synchronized + wait/notify`, or only `Mutex`? Say you prefer semaphores for turn-taking because they encode permits directly, but you can do it with one lock plus state. Interviewers who ban semaphores want the condition-variable version.

items.title: How do non-participating threads exit?
items.text: If `n=5`, the `even` thread has nothing to do on the last slot. Does it just return, or must it still participate in handshakes to avoid stranding `zero`? Agree that every thread must release the next owner even when it has no work, or that loops are bounded so extra threads terminate early without blocking others.

items.title: Interrupt and spurious wakeup policy?
items.text: Confirm methods may throw `InterruptedException` and that `wait()` must be in a `while` loop rechecking a predicate. If you state this upfront you earn the right to write `while (!myTurn) await()` without being challenged.

items.title: Output and visibility guarantees?
items.text: Confirm `printNumber` is the only output path and that happens-before between release and acquire is sufficient. You need shared state (`current i`, turn flag) to be guarded by the same lock or made volatile. Do not let the counter be a plain `int` read outside synchronization.

blocks.text: Requirements

blocks.caption: Scope agreed with the interviewer before writing any code.
rows: Emit 0,i for i=1..n in order, total 2n prints
Any deviation is a wrong answer, not a performance issue
Zero prints exactly before each i, never twice in a row
This forces alternation, not just mutual exclusion
Odd thread prints only odd i in order; even only even i
Prevents both number threads racing for the same slot
No deadlock, no missed signal, clean thread exit
Most failures are hangs on last iteration, not wrong digits
No busy spin; block in OS primitives
Spin-wasting CPU is a fail at senior level
O(n) prints, O(1) extra memory, O(1) work per handoff
Coordination must not dominate the work

blocks.text: Approach 1 — the naive approach and why it fails

The naive instinct is a single `synchronized` method plus a shared counter and an `if (turn == MINE)` check: each thread locks, checks if it is its turn, prints, bumps state, unlocks. Or worse, a `volatile boolean` with a `while` spin. It looks correct in a single happy-path trace and it passes if you test with sleeps. It collapses under a real scheduler. The trade-off you are ignoring is **simplicity vs. correctness under preemption**: without blocking and rechecking, you either burn CPU or lose ordering the moment two threads interleave between check and act.

blocks.title: Exactly why naive breaks
blocks.text: Three concrete failures: **1. Check-then-act race** — two threads both see `myTurn` true before either flips it. **2. No blocking** — a thread that arrives early either spins (100% CPU) or returns and drops its print. **3. No termination handshake** — when `n` is odd, `even` never runs last, so if `zero` blindly signals `even`, the permit dies and the system hangs. You need *permits*, not just exclusion, and the permit for slot `i` must go to exactly one number thread.
The real design — turn-taking with three semaphores

Model this as a token ring with a branch. `zeroSem` starts with 1 permit, `oddSem` and `evenSem` start with 0. `zero` acquires its own permit, prints `0`, then hands off to *exactly one* successor based on the upcoming `i`: if `i` is odd release `oddSem`, else release `evenSem`. That successor acquires, prints `i`, and releases `zeroSem` back. The trade-off is explicit: **three semaphores cost two extra objects versus one lock plus an int, but they make illegal states unrepresentable** — `odd` and `even` can never both be runnable because only one ever holds a permit. With a single lock you must encode that invariant by hand with `if/else` and you will get it wrong on the last iteration.

blocks.title: Permit flow
blocks.caption: Only one permit exists in the system at a time; zero routes it by parity.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  Z["zero: acquire zeroSem"] --> P["print 0, release oddSem if i odd else evenSem"]
  P --> O["odd/even: acquire own sem, print i"]
  O --> R["release zeroSem"]
  R --> Z

blocks.text: Why `zero` owns the routing decision: `zero` is the only thread that runs on every slot, so it is the only place that sees the full sequence `1..n`. Letting `odd` and `even` decide among themselves requires shared peek logic and an extra wakeup — more context switches and a classic lost-wakeup window. Centralising the branch in `zero` costs one conditional per iteration and buys deterministic handoff. The counter `i` itself is only touched by `zero` to choose the branch and by number threads to print in order, so sequence order falls out naturally if each number thread iterates its own arithmetic progression.
Class structure

blocks.title: Structure
blocks.caption: State is permits plus bound; no queue, no map, no extra threads.

classDiagram

    -int n
    -Semaphore zeroSem
    -Semaphore oddSem
    -Semaphore evenSem
    +ZeroEvenOdd(n : int)
    +zero(printNumber : IntConsumer)
    +even(printNumber : IntConsumer)
    +odd(printNumber : IntConsumer)
  }

blocks.text: Working code — Java with semaphores

Read the termination carefully because that is where candidates hang. `zero` always acquires before printing, so it cannot overrun. Each number thread loops only over its own parity, so for `n=5` the `even` loop runs twice and then returns — it never acquires a third time, which is correct because `zero` never releases `evenSem` a third time. The final action of the whole system is `odd` (or `even` when `n` is even) releasing `zeroSem`, but `zero` has already finished its loop and nobody else acquires, so one stray permit sitting in `zeroSem` at the end is harmless. The trade-off versus a barrier or `join` scheme: **you accept one leaked permit at shutdown to avoid a fourth shutdown handshake**, and that is strictly simpler and deadlock-free because no thread ever waits after its last print.
Same idea in Python
Complexity

blocks.caption: Cost of the semaphore handoff.
rows: Three semaphores plus bound; no per-i allocation
Two context switches per number; unavoidable for strict alternation
Trade-off vs spinlock: higher wake latency, near-zero wasted CPU
Scheduler cannot reorder; permits force the sequence

blocks.text: Concurrency correctness — the hardest follow-up

The interview pivots here: *do it with one `ReentrantLock` and two `Condition`s* or *prove no deadlock*. The semaphore version is deadlock-free by permit counting — there is always exactly one outstanding permit, held by whoever must run next, so no cycle is possible. But semaphores hide state, which is their weakness: you cannot inspect who should run without tracking `i`. The lock-plus-condition version makes the invariant explicit (`state = ZERO_TURN / ODD_TURN / EVEN_TURN` plus `current`) at the cost of more code and two classic traps. Trade-off to state out loud: **semaphores are shorter and less error-prone for fixed turn-taking; locks plus conditions generalise to arbitrary predicates like pause, reset, or multi-slot batching.** If the follow-up adds `reset()` or dynamic `n`, switch to the lock version without being asked twice.

blocks.title: Three traps that hang or corrupt
blocks.text: `if` instead of `while` around `await()` dies on spurious wakeup — always recheck. `signal()` instead of `signalAll()` with two waiters can wake the wrong parity thread, which re-waits and nobody else is awake to signal — prefer `signalAll()` unless you keep two separate conditions. And printing while *not* holding the lock breaks happens-before on `cur` — either print inside the lock (simple, slightly longer critical section) or copy `i` to a local and publish via volatile. Pick one and justify it.
Follow-ups to have ready

items.title: What if n is 10^9 or the stream is infinite?
items.text: Permits still work; memory stays O(1). The bottleneck becomes two context switches per element. Propose batching: zero prints k zeros then releases k permits, number threads drain. Trade-off: higher throughput, weaker per-element alternation guarantee.

items.title: Add a fourth thread that prints primes?
items.text: Do not add a fourth semaphore blindly. Generalise: zero routes by predicate to N conditions or a BlockingQueue of tasks. Semaphore-per-role scales as O(roles); a single lock plus state table scales better past three roles.

items.title: Handle interruption and cancellation?
items.text: Use interruptible acquire/await, never swallow InterruptedException. On interrupt, release whoever is next before exiting so survivors do not hang. Show the finally-release pattern.

items.title: Prove ordering under test?
items.text: Join all three threads, capture output in a synchronized StringBuilder, assert exact string for n=1,2,5,1000 and run with a stress loop plus Thread.yield. Mention testing with a barrier start so all threads race from the same instant.

items.title: Replace semaphores with lock-free code?
items.text: Say no for strict alternation. Lock-free turn flags still need parking (LockSupport.park) to avoid spin, at which point you rebuilt a semaphore badly. Lock-free wins for throughput, not for deterministic sequencing.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state unprompted

items: `n=1`: even thread must exit immediately without acquiring. Your `for (i=2; i<=1)` loop does that — say so.
`n=2`: odd runs once, even runs once. Final releaser is `even`. No extra acquire after.
Threads started in any order: initial permits `(1,0,0)` guarantee zero goes first even if odd/even start first and block.
Interrupt mid-wait: declares `throws InterruptedException`; never convert to infinite retry without re-interrupt.
Permit leak at shutdown: one unit left in `zeroSem` is intentional and harmless because no further acquire exists.
`printNumber` throwing: permits are lost unless you release in `finally`. Wrap print-then-release so an exception does not deadlock survivors.
Reuse of the instance for a second run: semaphores are single-shot here. State it — a second `start()` needs fresh instance or explicit reset under lock.

blocks.text: What you are graded on

blocks.caption: Weak vs strong signals for this concurrency LLD.
rows: Picks semaphores for turn-taking, names trade-off vs lock+condition
Single outstanding permit; zero routes by parity; stated as invariant
Blocks in acquire/await; zero CPU while waiting
Hangs on odd n; even thread waits forever

`if (await)`, print outside lock on shared state
Cannot adapt to 4 threads or reset
Switches to lock+state table when routing generalises

blocks.title: 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0-5 min:** clarify loops, primitives, exit policy. **5-10 min:** draw the permit ring and state the invariant. **10-25 min:** write the three-semaphore Java cleanly, narrate routing and termination. **25-35 min:** stress edge cases (`n=1`, wrong start order, interrupt) and prove no deadlock by counting permits. **35-45 min:** volunteer the lock-plus-condition rewrite and the batching / N-role generalisation. Close by saying when you would *not* use semaphores.
